solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Peak amount of weight besetting one chap with tankard maybe

indicators.note: to beset is to surround on all sides

parts.note: a kilo, a thousand grams
Roman numeral one
chap = man
a jar is a drinking vessel, and a jar of beer is a pint

explanation.surface: A mountaineer at the summit, weighed down by a companion clutching his beer mug.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Peak' looks like a high point of effort, but it is simply a mountain. 'Maybe' flags a tankard as just one example of a jar, a British word for a pint.
explanation.definitionFit: Kilimanjaro, in Tanzania, is Africa's highest peak.

clue.text: Oxford college mostly keen to embrace British Library

indicators.note: most of the word, so its last letter goes

parts.note: KEEN 'mostly' drops its final N
standard abbreviation for the British Library

explanation.surface: An eager Oxford college keen to take over the British Library's collections.
explanation.walkthrough: KEE opens as KE…E to take BL.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by category: Keble, founded in 1870 and named after the churchman John Keble, is one of Oxford University's colleges.

clue.text: Student revised Keats and Poe — part of English Literature syllabus?

parts.note: L, the learner plate, stands for a student

indicators.note: revised means reworked, so the letters of the two poets' names are rearranged

parts.note: the two poets' names joined together, KEATS and POE

explanation.surface: A student swots up on Keats and Poe for an English Literature course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'revised' rearranges KEATS and POE to AKEPOETS. Keats and Poe are poets, but neither was a Lake Poet; the Lake Poets were Wordsworth, Coleridge and Southey of the English Lake District.
explanation.definitionFit: The Lake Poets are the Romantic group studied on English Literature courses, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Top cyclist Rick dismissing current in Mexico

indicators.note: in places the shortened name inside the abbreviation for Mexico

parts.note: MEX is a standard abbreviation for Mexico

indicators.note: dismissing means sending away, so the letter for current is dropped from the name

parts.note: taken as written
I is the physics symbol for electric current

explanation.surface: A champion cyclist called Rick has sacked a member of staff while in Mexico.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rick' looks like the cyclist's first name, but he is Eddy; the name is only raw material, losing its current, while 'in' places the remainder inside the abbreviation for Mexico.
explanation.definitionFit: Eddy Merckx, the Belgian five-time Tour de France winner, is widely regarded as the greatest racing cyclist ever.

clue.text: Love characters regularly seen in Enfield

indicators.note: take letters at a regular interval: every second one

parts.note: e N f I e L d: the 2nd, 4th and 6th letters

explanation.surface: Romance glimpsed now and then in a north London suburb.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Love' looks romantic but is the tennis score, zero. Enfield is a borough of north London.
explanation.definitionFit: Love means zero in tennis scoring, and nil is zero.

clue.text: Strong drink curtailed all detective work

parts.note: ALL without its last L
cop = police officer
OP = opus, a work

explanation.surface: A hard-drinking detective whose investigation got cut short by the bottle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strong' is fair but a little cheeky: an alcopop is a sweet fizzy drink laced with alcohol.
explanation.definitionFit: An alcopop is an alcoholic soft drink, so a drink that is strong in the sense of containing alcohol.

clue.text: Six deliveries, arranged under bed, taxed excessively

indicators.note: the letters of UNDER BED are set in a new order

parts.note: in cricket an over is six balls bowled
anagram fodder, 8 letters

explanation.surface: A postman who has had to leave six parcels under someone's bed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Deliveries' suggests the post; in cricket a delivery is a ball bowled, and six of them make an over.
explanation.definitionFit: Overburdened means loaded, or taxed, beyond what one can bear.

clue.text: Iron withering piece of paper?

parts.note: to iron clothes is to press them
a withering remark is a cutting one

explanation.surface: A scorching iron shrivelling a sheet of paper.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark marks the pun: the piece is cut from a paper, meaning a newspaper, not just a sheet.
explanation.definitionFit: A press cutting is an article clipped from a newspaper, literally a piece of a paper.

clue.text: One who condemns beer drunk around our country run

indicators.note: a drunk thing is jumbled, so BEER's letters are rearranged
'around' means encircling, so the shuffled beer is wrapped round the country's letters

parts.note: BEER 'drunk', rearranged
the setter is British: the United Kingdom
R = run, from cricket scoring

explanation.surface: A critic who deplores all the beer drunk across Britain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Our country' is the setter speaking: a British puzzle, so it means the United Kingdom. The run is tacked on after the container is built.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym by derivation: to rebuke is to reprimand or censure, and the -er noun names the person doing it.

clue.text: Enticement to obtain constant riches

parts.note: a lure is a bait or enticement
c is the constant for the speed of light

explanation.surface: The eternal temptation of steady wealth.
explanation.walkthrough: LURE opens as LU…RE to hold C.
explanation.definitionFit: Lucre is money or riches, usually with a hint of disapproval.

clue.text: That woman records family's type of rug

parts.note: she = that woman
EPs are extended-play records
kin = family; the ’s reads as 'is', linking to the definition

explanation.surface: A woman's record collection laid out on the family's rug.
explanation.walkthrough: The ’s on 'family’s' does double duty in the surface; in the parse it just says the family pieces make up the rug.
explanation.definitionFit: A sheepskin, the fleece with its hide, is a common rug.

clue.text: Perhaps Titchmarsh in unusually sandy country once

indicators.note: in puts the gardener's first name inside the rearranged letters
unusually signals letters not in their usual order, so they are rearranged

parts.note: Alan Titchmarsh is a British TV gardener and presenter, an example of someone called Alan

explanation.surface: Alan Titchmarsh, the British TV gardener, finds himself in a strangely sandy land.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' marks Titchmarsh as just one example of an Alan; 'in' tucks that name into the shuffled sand letters rather than the gardener into a desert.
explanation.definitionFit: Nyasaland was the colonial name of the African territory that became independent Malawi in 1964.

clue.text: Some ibuprofen knocked back — after boozing here?

indicators.note: only part of the word is used
the letters run backwards, as a drink is knocked back

parts.note: the letters BUP sit inside iBUProfen

explanation.surface: Taking painkillers the morning after a night's drinking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Knocked back' suggests swallowing pills; it sends the hidden letters backwards. The definition is cryptic: the pub is where the boozing was done that calls for the ibuprofen.
explanation.definitionFit: A pub is where the boozing happens, and the question mark marks the playful definition.

clue.text: Companion welcome to join unknown South American revolutionary

parts.note: CH = Companion of Honour, a British order
ave, Latin for hail, a welcome
x, y and z are the algebraic unknowns

explanation.surface: A comrade invited to join a mysterious Latin American rebel.
explanation.walkthrough: Hugo Chávez, the Venezuelan leader, styled himself a Bolivarian revolutionary.
explanation.definitionFit: Hugo Chávez led an attempted coup in Venezuela and later a self-proclaimed revolution as president.

clue.text: Heard inheritor, Irishman, returning long-distance communication

indicators.note: the word is to be taken by its sound

parts.note: an inheritor is an heir, pronounced like 'air'
Liam, a typical Irish name

explanation.surface: An Irish heir sending word home from far away.
explanation.walkthrough: The silent H in HEIR is what makes it sound like AIR.
explanation.definitionFit: Airmail is post sent by aeroplane, typically over long distances.

clue.text: German agreed with second agent about gemstone

parts.note: ja is German for yes
s = second
a rep is a sales representative, an agent

explanation.surface: A German buyer striking a deal with a second dealer over a jewel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'German agreed' is one idea: the German word for agreement, JA.
explanation.definitionFit: Jasper is an opaque, often red, semi-precious stone.

clue.text: Question and answer primarily giving good advice for extinct creature

parts.note: QU = question

indicators.note: take the first letter of each following word

parts.note: A = answer
first letters of Giving Good Advice

explanation.surface: A question-and-answer session offering sound tips about a lost species.
explanation.walkthrough: The quagga is a rare word: a half-striped zebra of southern Africa, hunted out in the 1880s.
explanation.definitionFit: The quagga, a zebra subspecies, died out in the late 19th century.

clue.text: Seaman's thick black coat

definitions.meaning: old slang for a sailor, from the days of tarred pigtails and canvas
the sticky black substance, from coal or wood, spread as a coating on roads and ropes

explanation.surface: A sailor's heavy dark jacket.
explanation.walkthrough: TAR is old slang for a sailor, as in Jack Tar. 'Coat' looks like clothing belonging to the seaman; it is a coating. The ’s reads as 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Tar is old slang for a sailor, and tar is the thick black stuff used to coat roads and ropes.

clue.text: African pickle engrossing European person

parts.note: to souse is to pickle in brine or vinegar
a Dane, from Denmark

explanation.surface: An African in a pickle, absorbed by a European visitor.
explanation.walkthrough: SOUSE opens as SOU…SE to hold DANE. SOUDANESE is the old spelling of Sudanese.
explanation.definitionFit: Soudanese is an older spelling of Sudanese, a person from Sudan.

clue.text: Duck and fish in centre of mere

indicators.note: in places the fish inside the letters taken from the lake word
the centre of a word is everything but its outer letters

parts.note: a mere is a lake
the ide is a freshwater fish, also called the orfe

explanation.surface: A duck and a fish swim together in the middle of a lake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'centre of' takes ER from MERE, and IDE goes 'in' it.
explanation.definitionFit: The eider is a large sea duck, famous for the soft down it gives to eiderdowns.

clue.text: Unfit, sleep briefly surrounded by relations

indicators.note: to be surrounded by something is to have it on every side, so the short sleep is enclosed by the relations

parts.note: IT is a coy word for sex, as in sexual relations
to nap is to sleep for a short time

explanation.surface: Someone too unwell to cope, dozing off while the relatives crowd round.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Relations' looks like family, but is the euphemism: IT means sexual relations.
explanation.definitionFit: Inapt means unsuitable or unfit for the purpose.

clue.text: Group of workers book unwieldy boat

parts.note: TU = trade union
B = book

explanation.surface: A union booking a clumsy old boat for an outing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Book' reads as a verb, to reserve; it is just the abbreviation B.
explanation.definitionFit: A disparaging sense: a slow, broad, awkward boat is mockingly called a tub, as if it were a bathtub afloat.

clue.text: Doctor angered very important person

indicators.note: to doctor something is to tamper with it, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: anagram fodder, 7 letters

explanation.surface: A physician who has upset an important patient.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doctor' sits at the front looking like a noun, the one who angered; it is a verb telling you to tamper with ANGERED.
explanation.definitionFit: A grandee is a person of high rank or eminence.

clue.text: Part of body dance showing more happiness to Spooner

indicators.note: showing links the two words to the swap, presenting them as they would come out of Spooner's mouth
Spooner, the Oxford don famous for swapping the starts of words, signals that the opening sounds trade places

parts.note: a ball is a formal dance; said aloud it is the sound BAWL, and only the sounds are swapped
gladder means happier, showing more happiness

explanation.surface: A dance that brings more joy is somehow tied to an organ of the body.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to Spooner' swaps the opening B and G sounds of BALL (heard as BAWL) and GLADDER, and you hear GALL BLADDER; the swap is of sounds, so the L of GLADDER stays put.
explanation.definitionFit: The gall bladder is the small organ under the liver that stores bile, a part of the body.
